Name plans by their file, and read grommet's kinds quince

Quince read grommet's kinds and paired each Answered: with its Guess:, and it declined to pull the verdict out of the answer. Jeff asked for exactly that in sorrel's cart, so this plan stands where quince stood and asks its question again: how much of grommet's answer format should the page carry as structure?

Decision: What moved is our understanding, not the world or the code

where plans/2026-10-30-quince.md › Reading the verdict (held, disproved, not tested) out of an answer's prose

entry Decline: Reading the verdict (held, disproved, not tested) out of an answer's prose in quince

Because (Jeff and Claude): grommet already said an answer opens with held, disproved, partly disproved, or not tested when quince declined it. Quince read that as prose and called pulling a word out of it a guess. It's a convention with a closed set of four, which is structure written in words, like the Because (…) that marl now reads. What we learned was what it's for. "Which guesses are still open, and which were disproved?" is the question an agent arriving at code most needs answered, and today it takes two hops per guess (Jeff).

Decision: The verdict is the answer's first word or words, when they're one of grommet's four

where src/plan.ts file page

quote entry.source = /^\*\*(?:Because|Answer) \((.*?)\):\*\*/.exec(entry.body)?.[1];

Because (grommet, Jeff and Claude): after **Answer (…):**, the text starts with held, disproved, partly disproved, or not tested, followed by punctuation, a space, or the end. Anything after it ("as far as a dry run can tell," "on ten of ten") stays prose, where the reader sees it. Every answer in mock-control and phoropter opens this way today: six held and one disproved.

Decision: The verdict shows on the answer and on its guess

where src/render.ts file page

quote if (entry.answers) return `<p class="pair">Answers ${link('answers', 'answers', entry.answers, 'the plan’s guess')}.</p>`;

Because (Jeff): on the guess is where it's needed. A reader on a plan page sees "Answered in the as-built: held" without leaving the page, and one pass over the plan pages finds every guess that was disproved. Both carry itemprop="verdict". A guess with no answer has no verdict, which is how a reader finds the open ones.

Decision: An answer that doesn't open with one of the four says it has no verdict

Because (Claude, agreed by Jeff): the same as an answer with no matching guess. The page says so plainly rather than guessing at the prose.

Decline: Reading qualifiers, or a fifth verdict

Because (Claude): "held on what exists, and not yet tested against what would disprove it" is quince's own answer, and its first word is held. Reading on to decide it's really "not tested" would be the guess quince declined, and it would overrule the answer's author. The prose is right under it.

Guess: An answer's first word is the verdict its author meant

Answered in the as-built: held.

Disproved if: an answer opens with a verdict that its own prose contradicts, so that a reader trusting the structure would be misled. Quince's answer is the case to look at: "held," then "not yet tested."
